entry.title: [BIP Proposal] Anti-Fee-Sniping with LockTime
entry.summary:
The discussion on the BIP proposal and Anti-Fee-Sniping reveals several critical insights and updates regarding Bitcoin transaction policies and their implications. Initially, it is important to note that recent versions of Bitcoin Core no longer require BIP125 signaling for a transaction to be replaceable under the default mempool policy. This change could influence transaction handling practices significantly.
Concerning the Anti-Fee-Sniping mechanism, there are mixed implications for user privacy. Specifically, while the 10%-back-date-rule aims to enhance privacy by allowing fee-bumping of not previously back-dated transactions, this can inadvertently create a unique fingerprint. Such a fingerprint suggests that the replacement transaction might have been intentionally back-dated, as detailed in a reported issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/26526). Additionally, another concern raised involves potential edge cases that might not yet be fully explored or documented, which could lead to unintentional errors in future implementations ([GitHub Issue](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/26527)). Addressing these points within the BIP could prevent similar issues from arising in other contexts.
Moreover, practical challenges with implementing Anti-Fee-Sniping have been observed. For instance, a specific wallet attempting to implement this feature did not do so correctly, resulting in its transactions becoming easily identifiable, as discussed in an observation post from b10c ([Locktime Stairs Analysis](https://b10c.me/observations/01-locktime-stairs/)). Currently, this wallet is scarcely used, reducing the impact of this error ([Transactions Not Enforced Locktime](https://mainnet.observer/charts/transactions-not-enforced-locktime/)). However, only about 5% of transactions currently set a height-based time-lock, indicating that the practice of Anti-Fee-Sniping is not widely adopted. Expanding the anonymity set for transactions using time-locks might be beneficial, though it remains a niche area within the broader Bitcoin transaction landscape, as shown by the data from [Mainnet Observer](https://mainnet.observer/charts/transactions-height-based-locktime/).
These insights suggest a nuanced landscape of Bitcoin transaction policies, where adjustments to implementation and documentation could enhance both the functionality and security of digital transactions.
